In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Hal is used here in the sense of qad, specifically in the interrogative form, and the original is ahal, as evidenced by the line of poetry:

"Ahal ra'awna bi-saf'i al-qa'i dhi al-akam" [The explanation of this line of evidence was given in the third part, page 342, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come?" This is both an affirmation and an approximation together, meaning: "Has there come upon man, before a recent time, a period of time during which he was not a thing worth mentioning?" That is, he was a forgotten thing, not mentioned, a drop of sperm in the loins. The intended meaning of "man" is the species of the children of Adam, as evidenced by His saying: "Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled sperm."

A period of time: a portion of extended, long time.

If you ask: what is the place of "lam yakun shay'an madhkura" (he was not a thing worth mentioning)? I say: its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "man," as if it were said: "Has there come upon him a period of time in which he was not mentioned?" Or it is in the nominative as a description of "hin" (a period), like His saying: "a day when no parent will avail his child at all."

It is narrated from some of them that this verse was recited in his presence, and he said:

"Would that it had been completed," meaning: "Would that this state had been completed," which is his being a thing not worth mentioning, and not having been created and not having been obligated.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 76, verse 3:

*Shakiran* and *kafuran*: two circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in *hadaynāhu* [[Maḥmūd said: "They are two circumstantial accusatives referring to the pronoun in *hadaynāhu* ... etc." Aḥmad says: This is one of his objectionable distortions, and according to the Ahl al-Sunna it stands on its apparent meaning.]], that is: We empowered him and enabled him in both of his states together.

Or: We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, and it was known from him [[Maḥmūd said: "Or its meaning may be that We called him to faith, and it was known from him ... etc." Aḥmad says: His approval of the reading of Abu al-Sammāl stems from his imagining that the division indicates his corrupt purpose. It is not so, for the division allows for the recompense: either grateful, so he is rewarded, or ungrateful, so he is punished, and the mention of the recompense of the two groups afterward guides to this.]] that he would believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof against him.

It is also permissible that the two words are circumstantial accusatives referring to *al-sabīl* (the way), that is: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying *wa-hadaynāhu al-najdayn* (﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾). Describing the way with gratitude and ingratitude is figurative (majāz). Abu al-Sammāl read *innā* with a fatḥa on the hamza, and this is a good reading. The meaning is: as for the grateful, it is by Our enabling; as for the ungrateful, it is by his own bad choice [[His saying "by his own bad choice": this is according to the Mu'tazila's position that He, exalted is He, does not create evil. As for the Ahl al-Sunna, He is the creator of both good and evil, such as gratitude and ingratitude. (Ghayn)]].

When he had mentioned the two groups, he followed them with the threat and the promise. It was recited as *salasila* (سلاسل), without tanwin, and as *salasila* (سلاسلا), with tanwin.[[Mahmud said: "As for reciting *salasil* with tanwin, its explanation is that this nun is a substitute for the alif of extension (*alif al-itlaq*)... etc." Ahmad said: This is from the first rank, because his belief is that the widely transmitted recitations are not restricted to the mass-transmitted (*mutawatir*) report from the Prophet (ﷺ) in their details, and that they are left to the judgment of the reciters and their choice according to their own reasoning, as he has already mentioned. He has overlooked this here, so he treats the tanwin of *salasil* as one of the slips the tongue makes in a place where it does not belong, because it is accustomed to it in another place. The truth is that all the widely transmitted readings are transmitted by mass-transmission from him (ﷺ). The tanwin here is according to the dialect of those who apply tanwin in prose to every word that is not inflected (*ghayr munsarif*) except the form *af'al*. The readings include different dialects. As for *qawarir qawarir* (قوارير قوارير): it was recited without tanwin on both, which is the original form, and the tanwin on the first alone is a substitute for the alif of extension, because it is the pause-ending (*fasila*). The tanwin on the second, like the first, follows it. No one recited with tanwin on the second and without tanwin on the first, because that reverses the matter: it leaves out the tanwin of the pause-ending when there is a need for harmony, and applies tanwin to something else without need.]]. There are two explanations for it. The first is that this nun is a substitute for the vowel of extension, so that the connected reading takes the form of the pause. The second is that the reciter who recited it with tanwin was one who became accustomed to reciting poetry and whose tongue was trained to apply tanwin to what is not inflected.

The righteous (al-abrar) are the plural of barr or barr, like rabb and arbab, and shahid and ashhad. It is reported from al-Hasan [al-Basri] that they are "those who do not harm even an ant" [[His words "do not harm even an ant" – in al-Sihah, dharr means "ant." (Ed.)]]. A kas is a cup when it contains wine, and the term is also used for the wine itself. Mizajuha kafuran, "its mixture is camphor": it is mixed with camphor, which is the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is white like camphor, [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Kafuran is a spring in Paradise, named so because of its color, scent and coolness..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: This answer applies to the first two opinions. As for the other two opinions, that the spring is a substitute for the cup, the meaning of "its mixture is with camphor" would be either that it includes camphor's qualities, or that it is the familiar camphor, as mentioned earlier. In that case the answer given does not hold. The question may instead be answered by saying that since the drink was first mentioned in terms of its occurrence in existence, it is mentioned again to reassure the sense of enjoying it, as if to say: "They drink from it and so they enjoy it." Abu Ubayda interpreted it this way.]] its scent and its coolness. Aynan is a substitute for it. It is reported from Qatada: "It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk." It is also said: "Its scent, whiteness and coolness are created within it, so it is as if it were mixed with camphor." Ayn, on these two opinions, is:

a substitute for the place of min kas, with an omitted modifier, as if it were said: "They drink in it wine of a spring." Or it is in the accusative as a specification. If you ask: why is the verb of drinking first connected with the preposition of origin (min), and later with the preposition of attachment (bi)? I answer: because the cup is the starting point of their drinking and its first limit, whereas by the spring they mix their drink. So the meaning is: "The servants of Allah drink wine by it, as you say: I drank water with honey." Yufajjirunaha, "they make it gush": they channel it wherever they wish from their dwellings, tafjiran, easily, with nothing preventing them. Yufuna, "they fulfill," answers the question of one who might ask: "How do they obtain that?" The fulfilling of vows is an intensification in describing them as keen on performing obligations, because whoever fulfills what he has made obligatory upon himself for the sake of Allah will fulfill what Allah has made obligatory upon him. Mustatiran, "widespread": spreading, extending to the utmost extent, from istatara al-harig (the fire spread) and istatara al-fajr (the dawn spread). It is from tara, in the sense of istanfara min nafara (he was roused from his place). Ala hubbihi, "in spite of their love for it," refers to the food: that is, while they desire it and need it. Similar is ﴿and gives wealth out of love for it﴾ [2:177], and ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [3:92]. It is reported from al-Fudayl ibn Iyad that ala hubbihi means "out of love for Allah." Yatiman wa-asiran: al-Hasan said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be brought a prisoner, and he would hand him over to one of the Muslims, saying: "Treat him well." So the prisoner would stay with that man for two or three days, and he would give him precedence over himself. According to the majority of scholars, it is permissible to be kind to disbelievers within the abode of Islam, but obligatory charities are not directed to them. It is reported from Qatada: "Their prisoner on that day was a polytheist, but your Muslim brother has a greater right to be fed." It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ata: "He is a prisoner from among the People of the Qibla." It is reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "He is the slave and the imprisoned." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the debtor a prisoner, saying: "Your debtor is your prisoner, so be kind to your prisoner." Innama nut'imukum, "we feed you": this is with the intention of speaking. It may also be an utterance spoken aloud, to prevent them from repaying the favor with its like or with thanks, because their kindness is done for the sake of Allah, so there is no sense in seeking reward from creatures. It may also be that their words to them are gentleness, instruction and admonition, in accordance with what one who is sincere to Allah should be. It is reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to send charity to a household, then ask the Messenger what they had said. When he mentioned a prayer, she would pray for them in the same way, so that the reward of the charity would remain purely hers with Allah.

It may also be that this is a clarification and disclosure of their belief and the soundness of their intention, even if they did not say anything. It is reported from Mujahid: "Indeed they did not speak it, but Allah knew it of them, and so He praised them." Shukur and kufur are both verbal nouns like shukr and kufr. Inna nakhafu, "we fear": it may be that our kindness to you is out of fear of the severity of that Day, not out of desire for your repayment, and that we do not want repayment from you, fearing the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, for seeking repayment through charity.

Al-qamtarir: the intensely frowning one who gathers together the space between his eyes. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said iqmatarrat al-naqa when she raised her tail, gathered her two sides and closed her nostrils [[His words "gathered her two sides and closed her nostrils": al-qatr means side and direction. Zaqqa the bird fed its chick, meaning it fed it from its beak. Al-zaqra means bouncing a child. This is in al-Sihah. (Ed.)]], so he derived it from qatr and made the mim an augment. Asad ibn Na'isa said:

So war is likened to fire by way of implied metaphor (al-makniyya), and istilaʾ (warming oneself) is an imaginative evocation (takhyil). Basil means brave, when his frown is intense. ﴿And He has given them radiance and joy﴾, that is, in place of the frowning and sorrow of the wicked, He gave them radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts. They said: "O Abu al-Hasan, if you were to make a vow for your sons..." [[Al-Tha'labi related it from the narration of al-Qasim ibn Bahram from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and from the narration of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿They fulfil their vows﴾ (76:7), and he mentioned the whole of it, and he added verses of poetry by 'Ali and Fatimah within it. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said in his forty-fourth (chapter): Among the hadiths which hearts reject is a hadith they related from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and he mentioned it with its poetry. Then he said: This is a forged, fabricated hadith which only a foolish ignoramus would accept. Then he said: We have no doubt that it is fabricated.]], so 'Ali and Fatimah and their servant Fiddah vowed that if they both recovered from what they had, they would fast three days. They recovered, and they had nothing with them. So 'Ali borrowed three sa' of barley from Shim'un al-Khaybari, the Jew. Fatimah ground one sa', and baked five loaves according to their number. "Peace be upon you, people of the household of Muhammad. A poor man from among the poor of the Muslims. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the tables of Paradise." They preferred him, and they spent the night having tasted nothing but water, and they awoke fasting. When they reached the evening and placed the food before them, an orphan stood over them, and they preferred him. A captive stood over them on the third day, and they did the same. When they awoke, 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, took al-Hasan and al-Husayn by the hand and they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When he saw them trembling like chicks from the severity of hunger, he said: "How grievous it is to me to see what I see of you." He stood up and went with them, and found Fatimah in her prayer niche, her back stuck to her belly, and her eyes sunken. This distressed him, so Gabriel descended and said: "Take it, O Muhammad, may Allah bless you in your household," and he recited the surah to him.

If you ask: What is the meaning of mentioning silk along with the Garden? I say: The meaning is: "and He rewarded them for their patience in preferring others, and for what leads to it of hunger and nakedness, with a garden in which there is wholesome food, and silk in which there is fine clothing." That is, its air is temperate: there is no scorching heat of the sun, nor a painful severity of cold. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." [[His saying "the air of Paradise is sajsaj" — its explanation is what follows it, as al-Sihah indicates. (Ṣ)]] And it has been said: al-zamharir is the moon.

It is related from Tha'lab that it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited:

"And a night whose darkness had gathered, I crossed it while the moon did not shine."

[[That is: "And many a night whose darkness had accumulated, thickened and grown dense, I crossed it and passed through it by travelling, while the moon (al-zamharir) had not shone, i.e., had not appeared or given light. Al-zamharir in the dialect of Tayy means the moon, and this circumstance emphasizes the thickening of the darkness."]] The meaning is: Paradise is light, so there is no need in it for sun or moon.

If you ask: ﴿And its shades are close over them﴾ — on what is it conjoined? I say: It is conjoined to the sentence before it, because it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for those who are rewarded, and this is a circumstance similar to it, from them, due to the return of the pronoun from it to them in ʿalayhim (over them), except that this is a singular noun (ism mufrad), whereas that is a sentence which has the force of a singular noun, its estimate being: "not seeing in it a sun or a zamharir, and its shades close over them." The waw was introduced to indicate that both matters are gathered for them, as if it were said: "And He rewarded them with a garden, combining in it distance from heat and cold, and the nearness of shades over them." It has been read ﴿wa-daniyatan﴾ with raising (wa-daniyatun), on the basis that its shades are the subject (mubtada'), and daniyah is the predicate (khabar), and the sentence occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: "They do not see in it a sun or a zamharir, while its shades are close over them." It is also permissible to make ﴿reclining﴾ and ﴿they do not see﴾ and ﴿close﴾ all attributes of the garden. It is also permissible that ﴿wa-daniyatan﴾ be conjoined to ﴿jannah﴾, meaning: "and another garden whose shades are close over them," on the basis that they were promised two gardens, like His saying ﴿And for him who fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾ (55:46), because they were described as fearful: ﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord﴾ (76:10).

If you ask: On what is ﴿wa-dhullilat﴾ conjoined? I say: It is, if you raise ﴿daniyatan﴾, a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) conjoined to a nominal sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah). If you put it in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, then it is a circumstance of daniyah, meaning: its shades draw near to them in a state where its fruit-clusters are made easy for them to pick. Or it is conjoined to it, on: "its shades being close over them, and its fruit-clusters made easy." And if you put ﴿daniyatan﴾ in the accusative as an attribute, then it is an attribute like it. Do you not see that if you said: "a garden whose fruit-clusters are made easy," it would be correct? And the making easy of the clusters is that they are made docile, not refusing to be plucked however they wish. Or it means they are made humble for them, subdued and low, from the saying: "a wall is dhalil (low) if it is short."

﴿Qawarira, qawarira﴾ — they were read without tanwin, and with tanwin on the first, and with tanwin on both. This tanwin is a substitute for the alif of pronunciation (ilhaq), since it is a fasila (a pause-ending), and in the second it is for following the first. The meaning of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾ is that they are created from silver, and they, along with the whiteness of silver and its beauty, have the clarity and translucence of glass.

If you ask: What is the meaning of "kanat" (were)? I say: It is from "yakun" in His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾ (kun fa-yakun), meaning: the glasses came into being by Allah's creation, to magnify that marvellously wondrous creation which combines the two qualities of two disparate substances. And from it is kana in His saying ﴿Its mixture is camphor﴾ (76:5).

It has been read ﴿qawarir min fiḍḍah﴾ with raising, on: "they are glasses ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ (which they determined)," as an attribute of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾. The meaning of their determining it is that they determined it within themselves to be according to measures and shapes in accordance with their desires, and it came as they determined. And it has been said: the pronoun refers to those who go round with it, indicated by His saying ﴿and there go round among them﴾, on the basis that they determined its drink according to the measure of quenching, and this is more delicious to the drinker because it is according to his need, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It is related from Mujahid: "It neither overflows nor diminishes." And it has been read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ on the passive form (qudirrat) — its basis being that it is from qadara, transitively derived from qadara (to make able). You say: "I determined the thing, and so-and-so made it determined for me" (qaddarnīhi), when he makes you able over it. Its meaning is: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine it according to what they desired.

﴿And they are given to drink a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: the spring is named "zanjabil" because of the taste of ginger in it, and the Arabs find it delicious and pleasant.

Al-A'sha said:

"As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in its mouth, and honey from the hive, gathered."

[[By al-A'sha: he likened the smell and taste of her mouth to cloves and ginger, because the Arabs find them pleasant and delightful, and he likened the taste of her saliva to the taste of honey (al-aran), which is the honey. If you ask: ﴿And its shades are close over them﴾ — on what is it conjoined? I say: It is conjoined to the sentence before it, because it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for those who are rewarded, and this is a circumstance similar to it, from them, due to the return of the pronoun from it to them in ʿalayhim (over them), except that this is a singular noun (ism mufrad), whereas that is a sentence which has the force of a singular noun, its estimate being: "not seeing in it a sun or a zamharir, and its shades close over them." If you put it in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, then it is a circumstance of daniyah, meaning: its shades draw near to them in a state where its fruit-clusters are made easy for them to pick. And the making easy of the clusters is that they are made docile, not refusing to be plucked however they wish. Or it means they are made humble for them, subdued and low, from the saying: "a wall is dhalil (low) if it is short."

﴿Qawarira, qawarira﴾ — they were read without tanwin, and with tanwin on the first, and with tanwin on both. The meaning of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾ is that they are created from silver, and they, along with the whiteness of silver and its beauty, have the clarity and translucence of glass.

If you ask: What is the meaning of "kanat" (were)? It is related from Mujahid: "It neither overflows nor diminishes." And it has been read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ on the passive form (qudirrat) — its basis being that it is from qadara, transitively derived from qadara (to make able). You say: "I determined the thing, and so-and-so made it determined for me" (qaddarnīhi), when he makes you able over it. Its meaning is: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine it according to what they desired.

﴿And they are given to drink a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: the spring is named "zanjabil" because of the taste of ginger in it, and the Arabs find it delicious and pleasant.

Al-A'sha said:

"As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in its mouth, and honey from the hive, gathered."

[[By al-A'sha: he likened the smell and taste of her mouth to cloves and ginger, because the Arabs find them pleasant and delightful, and he likened the taste of her saliva to the taste of honey (al-aran), which is the honey. Al-mashur is a passive participle from sharahu sharran, when he picked it. Al-shur is the place where bees make honey.]]

And al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said:

"As if the taste of ginger in it, when I tasted it, and the wine's purest essence (sulafat al-khamr)."

[[By al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas. The word al-'alas in origin means the large tick, and by it the man was named, as in al-Sihah. (Ṣ) The application of the simile here to the taste of ginger indicates that it is so in the preceding verse. It is permissible that the pronoun "bihi" refers to the saliva, which is what is tasted, and the meaning of the sulafah being in it is that it is mixed in it.]]

Al-Zajjaj said: "Salsabil in the language is an attribute of what is in the utmost smoothness."

In the poetry of some later poets:

"Ask a way therein to the ease of the soul, with a wine as though it were salsabil."

He looked at it scattered on that carpet, admired the sight, and said: "By Allah, how excellent is Abu Nuwas!" It seems he had seen this when he said:

"As if the small and large of its bubbles were pearls scattered over a ground of gold."

[[By Abu Nuwas, describing wine: its bubbles which rise over it, like glass, resemble pearls, and it resembles gold; this is compound simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab). It is related that when Buran, daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was brought to al-Ma'mun ibn al-Rashid, he was on a carpet woven with gold, and the women of the caliphal house scattered pearls over it, so he looked at it and said: "How excellent is Abu Nuwas, when he said: 'As if the small...' (the verse)." It has also been said: they were likened to moist pearls when scattered from their shell, because it is the most beautiful and has the most lustre.

﴿And when you see﴾ has no manifest or estimated object, so that it may spread and be general, as if it were said: "And when you bring about sight, then..." Its meaning is that the sight of the beholder, wherever it falls, is not attached in its perception except to abundant bliss and great dominion. ﴿Thamma﴾ is in the position of an accusative of place (zarf), meaning "in Paradise." Whoever says its meaning is "mā thumma" (what is there) has erred, because "thumma" is a complement (ṣila) of "mā", and it is not permissible to drop the relative and leave the complement.

It is related that the least of the people of Paradise in station looks over his kingdom a distance of a thousand years, and sees its farthest end as he sees its nearest. It has been said: it has no cessation. It has been said: when they wish a thing, it comes to be. It has been said: the angels greet them and ask permission to enter upon them.

It has been read ﴿'āliyahum﴾ with sukūn (ʿāliyahum), on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿garments of green silk﴾. I say: Suppose it was said: "And they are adorned with bracelets of gold and of silver." This is correct and there is no difficulty in it, for they are adorned with both kinds, either by alternation, or by combination, just as the women of this world combine between various kinds of jewellery. And how fine it is that on the wrist there should be two bracelets: one of gold and one of silver.

[[His saying "the air of Paradise is sajsaj" — its explanation is what follows it, as al-Sihah indicates. (Ṣ)]] And it has been said: al-zamharir is the moon.

It is related from Tha'lab that it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited:

"And a night whose darkness had gathered, I crossed it while the moon did not shine."

[[That is: "And many a night whose darkness had accumulated, thickened and grown dense, I crossed it and passed through it by travelling, while the moon (al-zamharir) had not shone, i.e., had not appeared or given light. If you ask: ﴿And its shades are close over them﴾ — on what is it conjoined? I say: It is conjoined to the sentence before it, because it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for those who are rewarded, and this is a circumstance similar to it, from them, due to the return of the pronoun from it to them in ʿalayhim (over them), except that this is a singular noun (ism mufrad), whereas that is a sentence which has the force of a singular noun, its estimate being: "not seeing in it a sun or a zamharir, and its shades close over them." ﴿And they are given to drink a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: the spring is named "zanjabil" because of the taste of ginger in it, and the Arabs find it delicious and pleasant.

This is correct and there is no difficulty in it, for they are adorned with both kinds, either by alternation, or by combination, just as the women of this world combine between various kinds of jewellery. It has been said: it has no cessation. It has been said: when they wish a thing, it comes to be. It has been said: the angels greet them and ask permission to enter upon them.

It has been read ﴿'āliyahum﴾ with sukūn (ʿāliyahum), on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿garments of green silk﴾. [[Mahmud said: "It has been read with sukūn, on the basis that it is a subject whose predicate is 'garments...' etc." Ahmad said: In this other way there is a point to consider, for it makes it fall under the content of "hasibta" (you would think), and how can that be, when they are actually wearing green silk, not by way of likeness to pearls? And ﴿'āliyahum﴾ with fatḥah (naṣb) is on the basis that it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿yaṭūfu ʿalayhim﴾ or in ﴿ḥasibtahum﴾, meaning: young boys go round among them, above those who go round among them are garments. And ﴿istabraq﴾ has been read with naṣb in the position of the genitive, on the basis of prohibition of declension (man' al-ṣarf), because it is foreign (a'jamī); and this is an error, because it is indefinite, which the definite article can enter: one says "al-istabraq." ﴿And they are adorned﴾ (wa-ḥullū) is conjoined to ﴿and there go round among them﴾. If you ask: Here it is mentioned that their bracelets are of silver, and in another place that they are of gold. I say: Suppose it was said: "And they are adorned with bracelets of gold and of silver." This is correct and there is no difficulty in it, for they are adorned with both kinds, either by alternation, or by combination, just as the women of this world combine between various kinds of jewellery. And how fine it is that on the wrist there should be two bracelets: one of gold and one of silver.

﴿And He gave them to drink a pure drink﴾: not impure like the wine of this world, because its being impure is by the Law and not by reason, and the Abode is not an abode of obligation. Or because it was not pressed, so that dirty hands touch it, and filthy feet trample it, nor was it placed in jars and ewers which were not cared to be cleaned. Or because it does not turn into impurity, since it exudes a sweat from their bodies which has a scent like the scent of musk.

That is: it is said to the people of Paradise: ﴿Indeed this is﴾ — a reference to what was previously mentioned of Allah's bestowal upon them: "This is what you have been rewarded for your deeds, and your striving has been thanked," and "thanks" here is a metaphor (majaz).

﴿And He has given them radiance and joy﴾, that is, in place of the frowning and sorrow of the wicked, He gave them radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts. This indicates that the Day is described by the frowning of its people, ﴿because of their patience﴾, through their patience in preferring others (al-ithar).

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that al-Hasan and al-Husayn fell ill, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited them with some people who were with him. They said: "O Abu al-Hasan, if you were to make a vow for your sons..." [[Al-Tha'labi related it from the narration of al-Qasim ibn Bahram from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and from the narration of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿They fulfil their vows﴾ (76:7), and he mentioned the whole of it, and he added verses of poetry by 'Ali and Fatimah within it. Then he said: This is a forged, fabricated hadith which only a foolish ignoramus would accept. They placed them before them to break their fast, when a beggar stood over them and said:

"Peace be upon you, people of the household of Muhammad. A poor man from among the poor of the Muslims. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the tables of Paradise." They preferred him, and they spent the night having tasted nothing but water, and they awoke fasting. When they reached the evening and placed the food before them, an orphan stood over them, and they preferred him. A captive stood over them on the third day, and they did the same. When they awoke, 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, took al-Hasan and al-Husayn by the hand and they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When he saw them trembling like chicks from the severity of hunger, he said: "How grievous it is to me to see what I see of you." He stood up and went with them, and found Fatimah in her prayer niche, her back stuck to her belly, and her eyes sunken. This distressed him, so Gabriel descended and said: "Take it, O Muhammad, may Allah bless you in your household," and he recited the surah to him.

If you ask: What is the meaning of mentioning silk along with the Garden? I say: The meaning is: "and He rewarded them for their patience in preferring others, and for what leads to it of hunger and nakedness, with a garden in which there is wholesome food, and silk in which there is fine clothing." That is, its air is temperate: there is no scorching heat of the sun, nor a painful severity of cold. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." [[His saying "the air of Paradise is sajsaj" — its explanation is what follows it, as al-Sihah indicates. (Ṣ)]] And it has been said: al-zamharir is the moon.

It is related from Tha'lab that it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited:

[[That is: "And many a night whose darkness had accumulated, thickened and grown dense, I crossed it and passed through it by travelling, while the moon (al-zamharir) had not shone, i.e., had not appeared or given light. If you ask: ﴿And its shades are close over them﴾ — on what is it conjoined? It is also permissible to make ﴿reclining﴾ and ﴿they do not see﴾ and ﴿close﴾ all attributes of the garden. If you ask: On what is ﴿wa-dhullilat﴾ conjoined? I say: It is, if you raise ﴿daniyatan﴾, a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) conjoined to a nominal sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah). If you put it in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, then it is a circumstance of daniyah, meaning: its shades draw near to them in a state where its fruit-clusters are made easy for them to pick. Or it is conjoined to it, on: "its shades being close over them, and its fruit-clusters made easy." And if you put ﴿daniyatan﴾ in the accusative as an attribute, then it is an attribute like it. Do you not see that if you said: "a garden whose fruit-clusters are made easy," it would be correct? And the making easy of the clusters is that they are made docile, not refusing to be plucked however they wish. Or it means they are made humble for them, subdued and low, from the saying: "a wall is dhalil (low) if it is short."

﴿Qawarira, qawarira﴾ — they were read without tanwin, and with tanwin on the first, and with tanwin on both. This tanwin is a substitute for the alif of pronunciation (ilhaq), since it is a fasila (a pause-ending), and in the second it is for following the first. The meaning of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾ is that they are created from silver, and they, along with the whiteness of silver and its beauty, have the clarity and translucence of glass.

If you ask: What is the meaning of "kanat" (were)? I say: It is from "yakun" in His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾ (kun fa-yakun), meaning: the glasses came into being by Allah's creation, to magnify that marvellously wondrous creation which combines the two qualities of two disparate substances. It has been read ﴿qawarir min fiḍḍah﴾ with raising, on: "they are glasses ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ (which they determined)," as an attribute of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾. And it has been said: the pronoun refers to those who go round with it, indicated by His saying ﴿and there go round among them﴾, on the basis that they determined its drink according to the measure of quenching, and this is more delicious to the drinker because it is according to his need, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It is related from Mujahid: "It neither overflows nor diminishes." And it has been read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ on the passive form (qudirrat) — its basis being that it is from qadara, transitively derived from qadara (to make able). You say: "I determined the thing, and so-and-so made it determined for me" (qaddarnīhi), when he makes you able over it. Its meaning is: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine it according to what they desired.

﴿And they are given to drink a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: the spring is named "zanjabil" because of the taste of ginger in it, and the Arabs find it delicious and pleasant.

Al-A'sha said:

"As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in its mouth, and honey from the hive, gathered."

[[By al-A'sha: he likened the smell and taste of her mouth to cloves and ginger, because the Arabs find them pleasant and delightful, and he likened the taste of her saliva to the taste of honey (al-aran), which is the honey. Al-mashur is a passive participle from sharahu sharran, when he picked it. Al-shur is the place where bees make honey.]]

And al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said:

"As if the taste of ginger in it, when I tasted it, and the wine's purest essence (sulafat al-khamr)."

[[By al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas. The word al-'alas in origin means the large tick, and by it the man was named, as in al-Sihah. (Ṣ) The application of the simile here to the taste of ginger indicates that it is so in the preceding verse. The pronoun in bihi refers to the mouth; and "when I tasted it" means when I tasted its saliva, so it is a metaphor. Sulafat al-khamr is the first that is pressed from the grapes and begins to ferment. The taste of the saliva is likened to both in mere enjoyment, and does not imply that it has pungency as they both have. Sulafah is conjoined to "taste". It is permissible that the pronoun "bihi" refers to the saliva, which is what is tasted, and the meaning of the sulafah being in it is that it is mixed in it.]]

The meaning: it is in the taste of ginger, but without its sting; rather, it is the opposite of sting, namely smoothness. It is said: "a smooth drink (sharab salsal, salsal, salsabil)," and the letter ba' has been added in the structure until the word became quinquiliteral, and it indicates the utmost smoothness. Al-Zajjaj said: "Salsabil in the language is an attribute of what is in the utmost smoothness."

It has been read ﴿salsabīl﴾ without tanwin, on the basis of the combination of definiteness (al-'alamiyyah) and femininity (al-ta'nith). It has been attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that its meaning is "Ask a way to it" (sal sabīlan ilayhā). This is not correct in its outward meaning. Unless it is intended that the whole saying of the speaker, "sal sabīlan" (ask a way), was made a proper name for the spring, as it was said "Ta'abbaṭa sharran" and "Dharra Ḥubban", and it was named thus because no one drinks from it except one who asks a way to it by righteous deeds. This, though it is sound in Arabic, is affected and an innovation, and attributing it to a figure like 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, is an innovation.

In the poetry of some later poets:

"Ask a way therein to the ease of the soul, with a wine as though it were salsabil."

[[Seek a path in it to the rest of your soul, with "barrāḥ" — that is, with wine. Salsabil, salsāl, and salsal are a spring in Paradise, easy in descent in the throat, smooth in passage. The letter ba' was added for emphasis on smoothness and ease. Wine is likened to it because it is known and established among people that the drink of Paradise is the highest of drinks.]]

According to this view, ﴿a spring﴾ is a substitute for ﴿a cup﴾, as if it were said: "and they are given to drink in it a cup, a cup of a spring." Or it is in the accusative on the basis of specification (al-ikhtisas).

They were likened, in their beauty and the purity of their complexions, and their scattering in their assemblies and dwellings, to scattered pearls. It is related from al-Ma'mun that on the night Buran, daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was brought to him, he was sitting on a carpet woven with gold, and the women of the caliphal house had scattered pearls over it. He looked at it scattered on that carpet, admired the sight, and said: "By Allah, how excellent is Abu Nuwas!" It seems he had seen this when he said:

"As if the small and large of its bubbles were pearls scattered over a ground of gold."

It has also been said: they were likened to moist pearls when scattered from their shell, because it is the most beautiful and has the most lustre.

Or it means they are made humble for them, subdued and low, from the saying: "a wall is dhalil (low) if it is short."

﴿Qawarira, qawarira﴾ — they were read without tanwin, and with tanwin on the first, and with tanwin on both. This tanwin is a substitute for the alif of pronunciation (ilhaq), since it is a fasila (a pause-ending), and in the second it is for following the first. The meaning of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾ is that they are created from silver, and they, along with the whiteness of silver and its beauty, have the clarity and translucence of glass.

If you ask: What is the meaning of "kanat" (were)? I say: It is from "yakun" in His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾ (kun fa-yakun), meaning: the glasses came into being by Allah's creation, to magnify that marvellously wondrous creation which combines the two qualities of two disparate substances. And from it is kana in His saying ﴿Its mixture is camphor﴾ (76:5).

It has been read ﴿qawarir min fiḍḍah﴾ with raising, on: "they are glasses ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ (which they determined)," as an attribute of ﴿qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾. The meaning of their determining it is that they determined it within themselves to be according to measures and shapes in accordance with their desires, and it came as they determined. And it has been said: the pronoun refers to those who go round with it, indicated by His saying ﴿and there go round among them﴾, on the basis that they determined its drink according to the measure of quenching, and this is more delicious to the drinker because it is according to his need, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It is related from Mujahid: "It neither overflows nor diminishes." And it has been read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ on the passive form (qudirrat) — its basis being that it is from qadara, transitively derived from qadara (to make able). You say: "I determined the thing, and so-and-so made it determined for me" (qaddarnīhi), when he makes you able over it. Its meaning is: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine it according to what they desired.

﴿And they are given to drink a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: the spring is named "zanjabil" because of the taste of ginger in it, and the Arabs find it delicious and pleasant.

Al-A'sha said:

"As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in its mouth, and honey from the hive, gathered."

[[By al-A'sha: he likened the smell and taste of her mouth to cloves and ginger, because the Arabs find them pleasant and delightful, and he likened the taste of her saliva to the taste of honey (al-aran), which is the honey. Al-mashur is a passive participle from sharahu sharran, when he picked it. Al-shur is the place where bees make honey.]]

And al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said:

"As if the taste of ginger in it, when I tasted it, and the wine's purest essence (sulafat al-khamr)."

[[By al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas. The word al-'alas in origin means the large tick, and by it the man was named, as in al-Sihah. (Ṣ) The application of the simile here to the taste of ginger indicates that it is so in the preceding verse. The pronoun in bihi refers to the mouth; and "when I tasted it" means when I tasted its saliva, so it is a metaphor. Sulafat al-khamr is the first that is pressed from the grapes and begins to ferment. The taste of the saliva is likened to both in mere enjoyment, and does not imply that it has pungency as they both have. Sulafah is conjoined to "taste". It is permissible that the pronoun "bihi" refers to the saliva, which is what is tasted, and the meaning of the sulafah being in it is that it is mixed in it.]]

﴿And salsabil﴾: for the smoothness of its descent in the throat and the ease of its passage. The meaning: it is in the taste of ginger, but without its sting; rather, it is the opposite of sting, namely smoothness. It is said: "a smooth drink (sharab salsal, salsal, salsabil)," and the letter ba' has been added in the structure until the word became quinquiliteral, and it indicates the utmost smoothness. Al-Zajjaj said: "Salsabil in the language is an attribute of what is in the utmost smoothness."

It has been read ﴿salsabīl﴾ without tanwin, on the basis of the combination of definiteness (al-'alamiyyah) and femininity (al-ta'nith). It has been attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that its meaning is "Ask a way to it" (sal sabīlan ilayhā). This is not correct in its outward meaning. Unless it is intended that the whole saying of the speaker, "sal sabīlan" (ask a way), was made a proper name for the spring, as it was said "Ta'abbaṭa sharran" and "Dharra Ḥubban", and it was named thus because no one drinks from it except one who asks a way to it by righteous deeds. This, though it is sound in Arabic, is affected and an innovation, and attributing it to a figure like 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, is an innovation.

In the poetry of some later poets:

"Ask a way therein to the ease of the soul, with a wine as though it were salsabil."

[[Seek a path in it to the rest of your soul, with "barrāḥ" — that is, with wine. Salsabil, salsāl, and salsal are a spring in Paradise, easy in descent in the throat, smooth in passage. The letter ba' was added for emphasis on smoothness and ease. Wine is likened to it because it is known and established among people that the drink of Paradise is the highest of drinks.]]

﴿And a spring﴾ is a substitute for ﴿zanjabīlan﴾. It has been said: their cups are mixed with ginger itself, or Allah creates its taste in it.

According to this view, ﴿a spring﴾ is a substitute for ﴿a cup﴾, as if it were said: "and they are given to drink in it a cup, a cup of a spring." Or it is in the accusative on the basis of specification (al-ikhtisas).

They were likened, in their beauty and the purity of their complexions, and their scattering in their assemblies and dwellings, to scattered pearls. It is related from al-Ma'mun that on the night Buran, daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was brought to him, he was sitting on a carpet woven with gold, and the women of the caliphal house had scattered pearls over it. He looked at it scattered on that carpet, admired the sight, and said: "By Allah, how excellent is Abu Nuwas!" It seems he had seen this when he said:

"As if the small and large of its bubbles were pearls scattered over a ground of gold."

[[By Abu Nuwas, describing wine: its bubbles which rise over it, like glass, resemble pearls, and it resembles gold; this is compound simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab). It is related that when Buran, daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was brought to al-Ma'mun ibn al-Rashid, he was on a carpet woven with gold, and the women of the caliphal house scattered pearls over it, so he looked at it and said: "How excellent is Abu Nuwas, when he said: 'As if the small...' (the verse)." He was criticized for using "sughra" and "kubra" (small and large) unaccompanied by the article (al-) and without an annexed noun, although they are derived from the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil), and when such a form is used unaccompanied, it must be masculine.]]

It has also been said: they were likened to moist pearls when scattered from their shell, because it is the most beautiful and has the most lustre.

﴿And when you see﴾ has no manifest or estimated object, so that it may spread and be general, as if it were said: "And when you bring about sight, then..." Its meaning is that the sight of the beholder, wherever it falls, is not attached in its perception except to abundant bliss and great dominion. ﴿Thamma﴾ is in the position of an accusative of place (zarf), meaning "in Paradise." Whoever says its meaning is "mā thumma" (what is there) has erred, because "thumma" is a complement (ṣila) of "mā", and it is not permissible to drop the relative and leave the complement.

﴿A great kingdom﴾: spacious, pleasant. It is related that the least of the people of Paradise in station looks over his kingdom a distance of a thousand years, and sees its farthest end as he sees its nearest. It has been said: it has no cessation. It has been said: when they wish a thing, it comes to be. It has been said: the angels greet them and ask permission to enter upon them.

It has been read ﴿'āliyahum﴾ with sukūn (ʿāliyahum), on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿garments of green silk﴾. [[Mahmud said: "It has been read with sukūn, on the basis that it is a subject whose predicate is 'garments...' etc." Ahmad said: In this other way there is a point to consider, for it makes it fall under the content of "hasibta" (you would think), and how can that be, when they are actually wearing green silk, not by way of likeness to pearls? Unlike their being pearls, which is by way of simile, requiring their resemblance to pearls to be close enough that they might be thought pearls. It may be allowed that this way is sound, but only after a strain that is dispensed with by the first.]] Its meaning is: what is above them of their clothing is garments of green silk. And ﴿'āliyahum﴾ with fatḥah (naṣb) is on the basis that it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿yaṭūfu ʿalayhim﴾ or in ﴿ḥasibtahum﴾, meaning: young boys go round among them, above those who go round among them are garments. Or: "you thought them pearls, above them are garments." It is also permissible that the meaning is: "you saw people of bliss and dominion, above whom are garments." It has been read ﴿'āliyatihim﴾ with raising and with fatḥah on that basis. And ﴿'alayhim﴾ and ﴿khuḍr﴾ and ﴿istabraq﴾ with raising, treating them as conjoined to ﴿thiyāb﴾ (garments), and with the genitive on ﴿sundus﴾.

And ﴿istabraq﴾ has been read with naṣb in the position of the genitive, on the basis of prohibition of declension (man' al-ṣarf), because it is foreign (a'jamī); and this is an error, because it is indefinite, which the definite article can enter: one says "al-istabraq." Unless Ibn Muhaysin claims that it has been made a proper name for this kind of garment. It has also been read ﴿wa-istabraqa﴾ with a connecting hamza and fatḥah, on the basis that it is named with the form istaf'al from al-bariq (sheen), and this is also not correct, because it is a well-known arabized word, and its origin is "istabrah."

﴿And they are adorned﴾ (wa-ḥullū) is conjoined to ﴿and there go round among them﴾. If you ask: Here it is mentioned that their bracelets are of silver, and in another place that they are of gold. I say: Suppose it was said: "And they are adorned with bracelets of gold and of silver." This is correct and there is no difficulty in it, for they are adorned with both kinds, either by alternation, or by combination, just as the women of this world combine between various kinds of jewellery. And how fine it is that on the wrist there should be two bracelets: one of gold and one of silver.

﴿And He gave them to drink a pure drink﴾: not impure like the wine of this world, because its being impure is by the Law and not by reason, and the Abode is not an abode of obligation. Or because it was not pressed, so that dirty hands touch it, and filthy feet trample it, nor was it placed in jars and ewers which were not cared to be cleaned. Or because it does not turn into impurity, since it exudes a sweat from their bodies which has a scent like the scent of musk.

That is: it is said to the people of Paradise: ﴿Indeed this is﴾ — a reference to what was previously mentioned of Allah's bestowal upon them: "This is what you have been rewarded for your deeds, and your striving has been thanked," and "thanks" here is a metaphor (majaz).

Repetition of the pronoun after it is placed as the subject of inna: an emphasis upon an emphasis, for the meaning of God's exclusive authority over the revelation, so that it is settled in the soul of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that, since He is the One who sent it down, its sending down in whatever manner it came was nothing but wisdom and rightness. It is as if it were said: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you in gradual installments (tanzil mufarraqan munajjaman) except that I, and no other, did so. You have known Me as Wise, one who does everything I do for the sake of wisdom. Indeed, a profound wisdom has prompted Me to send down upon you the command to endure and to persevere, and I will send down upon you the command to fight and to take vengeance after a while. So be patient with the judgement of your Lord, which proceeds from wisdom and from linking affairs to their benefits, and with His delaying your victory over your enemies from the people of Makkah. And do not obey any of them, [this being said] because of your lack of patience with their harm and your impatience at the delay of victory." 

They, despite their excess in enmity and in harming him and those with him, would ask him to give up his affair, offering him their wealth and marriage to their most noble daughters if he agreed to them.

If you say: "They were all disbelievers, so what is the meaning of the division in His words, 'sinful or ungrateful'?" I say: its meaning is, "Do not obey any of them who is committing sin and who calls you to it, or who is doing what is disbelief and calls you to it," because they would either call him to assist them in an act that is sin or disbelief, or in something that is neither sin nor disbelief. So he was forbidden to assist them in the two but not in the third.

It is also said: "The sinful one" refers to Utbah, and "the ungrateful one" to al-Walid, because Utbah was constantly engaged in sins, pursuing all kinds of wickedness, and al-Walid was predominantly in disbelief, very stubborn in his obstinacy.

If you say: "The meaning of 'or' is: do not obey either of them; why was 'and' not used instead, so that it would be a prohibition against obeying both of them together?" I say: if it had been said, "Do not obey them," it would be permissible to obey one of them. But when it is said, "Do not obey either of them," it is understood that the one forbidden from obeying either of them is forbidden from obeying both together, a fortiori. Just as when one is forbidden to say "uff" to his parents, it is understood that he is forbidden from striking them, by way of a fortiori reasoning.

﴿And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening﴾, and persist in the prayer of dawn and afternoon. ﴿And during the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long part of the night﴾: perform the tahajjud for Him during a long portion of the night, that is, two-thirds of it, or half of it, or a third of it. Or it means the maghrib and 'isha' prayers, and "min" is used with the adverbial noun to indicate partiality, just as it is used with the object in His words, ﴿that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾.

Indeed, these disbelievers love the fleeting (worldly life) and prefer it over the Hereafter, like His saying: ﴿Nay, you prefer the life of this world.﴾ ﴿And they leave behind them a heavy day﴾: "behind them" means in front of them, or behind their backs; they pay no heed to it. The word "heavy" (thaqil) is used metaphorically for its severity, and it is heavy upon them, from the heavy thing that is burdensome to its carrier. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿It has been heavy in the heavens and the earth.﴾

Al-Asr (al-asr) means binding and fastening. From it: "asara al-rajul" when a man is bound tightly with rawhide, and that is al-isar (the binding). A horse is described as "ma'sur al-khalq" (well-knit in its structure), and a shield is "ma'sur bi-l-aqib" [[The saying "wa-tars ma'sur bi-l-aqib": in the Sihah (of al-Jawhari), "al-aqib," with a vowel on the qaf, is the sinew from which bowstrings are made; its singular is "aqibah." You say of it: "aqibtu al-sahm wa-l-qadah wa-l-qaws" when you twist something of it around the arrow, the arrow-shaft, or the bow. (Editor's note: this is the annotation within the text.)]]. The meaning is: We strengthened the joining of their bones to one another, and the fastening of their joints with sinews. Similar to it is their saying: "jariyah ma'subat al-khalq wa-majdulatuhu" (a girl well-knit and firmly constructed in her frame).

This is a commentary on surah 76, verses 29–31.
